title: Claude Shannon Predicts the Next Letter (1951)
explainer: A few years after founding information theory, Claude Shannon ran a strikingly simple experiment: have a person guess the next letter of an English passage, one letter at a time, to measure how predictable — and therefore how redundant — the language really is. His 1951 paper 'Prediction and Entropy of Printed English' is the direct conceptual ancestor of the next-token-prediction objective that trains every modern LLM, decades before anyone imagined running it on a neural network.

title: Zipf's Law and the Long Tail of Language (1949)
explainer: Linguist George Kingsley Zipf formalized, in his 1949 book 'Human Behavior and the Principle of Least Effort,' an empirical pattern already noticed by earlier researchers: in any natural-language corpus, a word's frequency is roughly inversely proportional to its rank, so a handful of words dominate while most words are rare. This skewed distribution is exactly why LLMs use subword tokenization rather than whole-word vocabularies — without it, the long tail of rare words would either blow up the vocabulary or leave the model with almost no training signal for most of it.
